utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. You're continuing examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Pisarevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you all. Good afternoon, Mr. Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we talked about the way the 4th Detachment was organised and so on. Before we continue talking about the same subject, I will ask you a question related to the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group. How far did the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group spread to the west? Where was its western boundary?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area or zone of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group in the west was as far as the Modrica local commune boundary, the Bosna River, and then all the way up to the river Sava.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please just tell us: Which bank of the river Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right-hand side of the river Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us: The 4th Detachment, did it have in its possession any communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The detachment only had one radio station, which was kept at the command of the detachment, but it had no communications equipment other than that. And this was used to establish communication with the command of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us anything about how the materiel supplies for the detachment were taken care of? Hereby I mean weapons and the remaining equipment.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the equipment necessary for any detachment, the 4th Detachment or any other detachment, the commanders of companies would draw up lists of necessary materiel and necessary equipment, and then this equipment would be obtained from the logistics detachment, under the command of the 17th Tactical Group. And if the equipment was available, then it would immediately be sent to the detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the detachments have their own warehouses where military equipment and weapons were being kept?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't have their own storages or warehouses. They didn't keep any equipment in any warehouses because they had no warehouses to begin with. Usually the commands -- I was speaking about the 4th Detachment for example, was located at the Sit factory, and other commands were located at local communes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. I'd just like to ask the witness one question. So in terms of logistics and so on, are you aware and were you involved with Mr. Miroslav Tadic in connection with his task as being assistant commander for logistics for the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no cooperation with Miroslav Tadic. My job was not related to the supply of technical equipment from the logistics unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, do you know how, in what way, members of the 4th Detachment, or other detachments, signed for military equipment or weapons? If you know, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the procedure how weapons were signed for in the 4th Detachment or any of the other detachments, only that there were problems with -- different --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He says he's familiar with the procedure. Is he talking generally that he's familiar with the military procedure or is he saying that he has personal knowledge as to the method that the 4th Detachment used? And it's not clear from the question or from his answer, and that's why I objected at that point. Because it's not going to be clear for you, if he's just going to be explaining how his knowledge from his many years in the military, how the procedure works, that's one thing; it's another thing to say: I know exactly how it worked within the 4th Detachment because I was involved with their logistics procedures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the question can be more specific, to also illustrate the basis of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to do so, but I would just like to add that my learned friend and colleague should not forget that Mr. Makso, in terms of his position, was chief for security in the 17th Tactical Group. Weapons are no toys. So of course the chief of security would be informed about such issues. My question to Mr. Simeunovic was whether he personally had any knowledge as to what the procedure was for obtaining weapons for detachments of the JNA, all those that were part of the 17th Tactical Group. As we have said, the detachments had no warehouses, no storages, had no weapons being kept there, so I think it's best to just to leave this to the witness to say what knowledge he has of that, because I think he may have accurate knowledge concerning that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to him asking the question; I'm just trying to find out if he has personal knowledge. I have -- I'm not objecting to the issue being raised under the issue of relevance. I just want the question clarified as to what his personal knowledge is about the 4th Detachment, or at least explain whether he's talking about his general military knowledge or his specific knowledge relating to the situation in the 4th Detachment. That's all. So there's no misunderstanding here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure the witness will be able to answer that, now that it's been explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can provide an accurate answer as to how, in what way, members of the 4th Detachment obtained weapons. I was there, after all. I was an eyewitness to this process. Following mobilisation call-up to the JNA, those who responded to the call-up, that was registered, and then shooting practice using infantry weapons would be organised. And before that, the men would have been trained to use those weapons. So after shooting practice, which was done at the firing range belonging to the JNA in Potocari, Brcko municipality, where shooting practice with infantry weapons is usually performed for units belonging to the 395th Motorised Brigade, so those people would already have been trained to use those weapons. And upon completion of the shooting practice, they would be issued with permissions signed by the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, permissions to be in possession of said weapons, with serial numbers, registration numbers, and so on and so forth, and then they would take these weapons home. They wouldn't leave these weapons in any warehouses of the 4th Detachment, because the 4th Detachment had no warehouses. Only their attention was drawn to the way in which they should keep these weapons at home. They were told that the weapons were to be kept in a safe place outside the reach of especially children, or any other persons not trained to use those weapons. They were told that they could not keep the ammo in the same place as the weapons, but rather, that ammunition was to be kept separately. They were provided all these explanations. That's when they were also informed about sanctions that would be imposed in case of failure to comply with these orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your personal knowledge, can you tell us: Which weapons were the weapons for the 4th Detachment or other detachments? Were those infantry weapons or other kinds of military equipment?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the 4th Detachment and the other detachments, they only had infantry weapons. They didn't have any artillery. The only thing they had was personal infantry weapons that each JNA soldier would be expected to carry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those detachment members who had responded to the mobilisation call-ups, were they given salaries for being members of the detachment, or any other form of reward?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not a single member who responded to the mobilisation call-up - and this goes for both the 4th Detachment and all the other detachments - was given any compensation or salary, because they were going after their regular duties in their regular jobs, companies. They had agricultural tasks or they worked for private companies. But the JNA certainly didn't give them any form of compensation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of the ethnic structure of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the 4th Detachment was of a mixed make-up. It included Muslims, Serbs, and Croats. This was at its most obvious in the 4th Detachment, of all the infantry detachments, because most of the other detachments were predominantly Serb, with the exception of the armoured battalion, which was also mixed. But that was only up to the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Can you please tell us, if you know: What was the area of responsibility of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I could tell you. I may not be able to tell you accurately what the area of responsibility was, but I know according to the assignments where the 4th Detachment was based, where its command, the area of responsibility was. That's the right hand bank of the river Bosna, in front of the river Sava, to the left -- that's to the right, the eastern section, as far as the border of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question related to the same subject. These detachments, did they comprise local population for each of these detachments?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Yes. Beginning with the commander, the command itself, the detachment command. All members of the detachment were locals, with the exception of the armoured battalion, because that was a particular case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we'll switch to a different subject, which is also related to established detachments. So please, if you can, answer. What was the formational organisation of the -- of a detachment of the JNA? What did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All detachments that were part of the 17th Tactical Group consisted of the detachment's command, they consisted of infantry companies of the JNA, and then there was -- this was purely formal at the beginning, because there was no warehouse to begin with. But a part of it would have been a logistics company too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the command of a detachment really, in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. I wonder, witness, whether you would be able to indicate, when you say "there was no warehouse to begin with." So where were the weapons stored for the 4th Detachment and the other detachments which formed part of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to answer that question a little bit earlier. Perhaps I wasn't understood. The weapons in the possession of the members of the 4th Detachment, which we're talking about, but this applies to all the other detachments too, after they were issued with weapons, after training, after firing practice, they took their own personal weapons home and they kept those at home. I explained that they were given a warning about the way they should keep those weapons at home and how they must maintain them. There were no warehouses that belonged to the detachments. There wasn't any space where weapons were kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, witness. I do recall you mentioning that exactly, but it was just your answer just before my question which then, shall we say, confused your first answer a little bit, because on page 7, lines 18 to 22, you talk about -- well, you say there: "There was no warehouse to begin with, but part of it would have been a logistics company too," and that really made -- maybe it's a question of translation, but it made no real sense to me, so hence my question as to what this answer actually meant. But maybe Mr. Pisarevic can clarify that with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was all the materiel, technical, and combat equipment kept which was at the disposal of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All equipment of the 17th Tactical Group, except for the armoured battalion, was kept in warehouses at the command of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please tell us where these warehouses were and what this place is called.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The warehouses were in the village of Krepsic, the municipality of Brcko. This is where the equipment of the 17th Tactical Group was located, and they were under guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after this training that you spoke about, when did the members of the detachment receive weapons; and when that happened, where were the weapons brought from to the place where the training was held and where it was issued to the members?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons were brought from the warehouses to the place where these units reported to, and this is where the weapons were issued and where training was carried out in the use of these personal infantry weapons. And then firing practice was conducted. So the weapons were first distributed and then they had target practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have one more question regarding that. Did the commanders of the detachments and their deputies for rear -- for logistics, did they have any access to the warehouses where the weapons were kept?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not have access whenever they wished. They would write up requests stating how many weapons they needed, depending on the number of persons who responded to the call-up. For example, if on a certain day they needed 50 rifles, the requests would be sent to the command of the 17th Tactical Group, and then somebody from the logistics would go to the warehouse, they would take the equipment, and then issue this equipment to the commanders at the place where the detachment reported to, and then the commanders would issue that to the conscripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So nothing from those warehouses could be taken without the assistant commander for the rear or for logistics of the 17th Tactical Group, without his knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't possible. You needed to have a special pass in order to enter the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that now we have clarified this point. Very well. You said a little earlier something about the formation and the organisation of the detachment. Could you please tell us: What functions were part of the detachment command? What comprised this command?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, so from the period when these people were called up, the command of the detachment comprised the commander, the deputy commander, there was the assistant commander for intelligence and security issues, the assistant commander for logistics was there also, then a communications officer, who maintained communications. These were soldiers who would switch. So this was the inner command. Then later, when you switched -- when you moved into the battalions, then this was a little broader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, we're now talking about the detachments. We're still talking about 1991 and 1992, up to April 1992. And you've already said that the commander of the 4th Detachment was Reserve Captain Radovan Antic.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was the deputy of the commander of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputy commander was also a captain. His name is Jovo Savic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who was the assistant commander in the logistics unit?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we will talk about the functioning and the principles of command within the Yugoslav People's Army, and my first question is: Who could issue orders to the 17th Tactical Group of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders in the 17th Tactical Group could be issued by the commander and the deputy commander, in the absence of the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, or the person who was the chief for intelligence and security issues -- were you able to issue commands on behalf of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As assistant commander of the chief for intelligence and security could not issue executive orders. I could only propose to the commander certain things, and then after assessment, he would adopt them. And then in his order he would take into account these suggestions of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Something which is a little bit ambiguous in page 11, line 9. The question of my learned friend Mr. Pisarevic was: "Who could issue orders to the 17th Tactical Group?" And the answer is: "Orders in this 17th Tactical Group could be issued" et cetera et cetera. So I believe that it's not so clear whether it's the issue of the orders of the Superior Command to the 17th Tactical Group or the question was related the orders within 17th Tactical Group, where that answer could be related. Maybe we could clarify that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Pisarevic will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness and I understood one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me: On behalf of the 17th Tactical Group, who could issue orders, executive orders?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To repeat again: On behalf of the 17th Tactical Group, executive orders could be issued by the commander of the 17th Tactical Group; in his absence, the orders could be issued by the chief of the staff, because according to his function, he stood in for the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've clarified now your role as the chief of intelligence and security issues. Could you please tell me now: Who in the 4th Detachment, and in other detachments, could issue executive orders on their behalf?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army functioned according to the principles of subordination. So in the detachments, executive orders could be issued by the commander and, in his absence, the deputy commander of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any authority or the possibility -- did the assistant commander for intelligence and security have the authority or the possibility to issue orders?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He could not have such authority to issue executive orders. Just on the basis of his information, he could make proposals or suggestions to his commander. The commander was the only one who could issue an executive order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is just one small clarification for the transcript. On page 12, line 21, instead of -- last word of the sentence, the deputy of the commander instead of deputy of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned one principle according to which the Yugoslav People's Army was structured and according to which it functioned. Could you please explain whether there were any other principles according to which the army functioned, except for the one of subordination? Could you please explain to us what singleness of command means? Could you please explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understood the question, and if I understood it properly, executive orders could be issued only by the commander. However, a specific characteristic of intelligence and security organs within the JNA is that they are a little different. They function along two lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will discuss that later. Did the commander of the 4th Detachment have the power to engage the detachment without the order of the commander of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he couldn't independently engage the detachment or a part of the detachment, the 4th Detachment, his detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber: How did the security and intelligence organs function? You already started to tell us something about that. Could you please describe these specific characteristics? What are they?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant commander for intelligence and security in the detachment was subordinated to the commander of the detachment, but he was also subordinated to the chief of the brigade or, in this case, of the 17th Tactical Group, so to the chief for intelligence and security. The assistant commander in the detachment was not obliged to convey to the detachment commander all the information he had, and particularly not his source of information. When he did have such information, he would submit his proposal to the commander. The commander would assess that and, in his order, would incorporate a part or all of this proposal. The assistant commander for security and intelligence was obliged in this case to send me all information, as the chief of intelligence and security of the 17th Tactical Group. So he would send all the information to me, and he was obliged -- he was not obliged to tell me his sources of information either, because it was his duty to protect the confidentiality of the person that he obtained the information from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, you were just like the commander of the 4th Detachment, the superior to Mr. Simo Zaric, who was carrying out the function of assistant commander for security and intelligence in the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was his superior officer, according to the intelligence/security line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you received a report by the assistant commander for intelligence and security from the detachment, were you obliged to inform the assistant commander of the detachment of what happened as a result of that report? Could you please explain how this functioned.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I would receive regular reports, daily regular reports from all of the assistant commanders, it was my task to assess these reports, compile my report for the Superior Command, to give suggestions to my commander based on those reports, which he would then use in his duties. But I did not have the obligation to inform the deputy -- the assistant commanders about what I -- what steps I took as a result or based on their reports. I was not obliged to convey this information to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were a direct superior to Mr. Zaric, especially as concerns security, can you tell us: What was the cooperation like? How did Mr. Zaric go about his task in the 4th Detachment, in the area of intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cooperation with Simo Zaric, who was the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the 4th Detachment, was good. I can even go so far as to say that this cooperation was excellent. All the tasks that I gave him, Simo Zaric carried out in a responsible and timely manner. Simo was - not was, is - a Yugoslav by conviction. He advocated those ideas and carried out those tasks which the JNA stood for. He was a good person to work with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us: At that time, what were the fundamental goals and tasks of the JNA and the 4th Detachment or the 17th Tactical Group, which were part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I would choose not to talk specifically about the tasks of the JNA, generally, but the tasks of the 17th Tactical Group or the 4th Detachment, or any of the other detachments. That's something I can indeed tell you about. Those were primarily tasks concerning the prevention -- we were in charge of preventing the war from spreading into Bosnia-Herzegovina, because our area of responsibility was on the border. That was our most fundamental task. Our next task was, in case there were violations or interethnic strife which might result in great casualties, the 4th Detachment could be used for the separation of the ethnic groups in conflict, but the 4th Detachment was not meant to fight on anyone's behalf. So the main task of the JNA was to serve as a buffer zone, in a manner of speaking, between the parties in conflict, in order to ensure the conditions for a political solution at some later stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber: Who was the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the 1st Detachment of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 1st Detachment of the 17th Tactical Group, with headquarters in the village of Batkusa, Bosanski Samac municipality, the assistant commander for intelligence and security was Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about your cooperation with Mr. Stevan Todorovic, as assistant commander for the 1st Detachment for intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Could we find out the dates when Mr. Todorovic held that position?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Honourable Court during which period of time Stevan Todorovic acted as the assistant commander for intelligence and security of the JNA's 1st Detachment? Which period of time are we referring to?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was towards the end of 1991. That's between the time the 17th Tactical Group was established, between the time the 1st Detachment was established, and April 1992. That is the specific time period we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about your cooperation with him, with Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unlike what I told you about my cooperation with Simo Zaric, my cooperation with Stevan Todorovic was very different when he was the assistant commander for intelligence and security. He simply didn't respect me in my position as the chief. But it was only -- it was not only the case with me. He didn't have any respect for most of his superiors. He said that they were Tito's soldiers and that they should go away. All those who were Yugoslavs by conviction, he called them Tito's soldiers, and he said all these people should be made to go away. As far as our cooperation on security and intelligence tasks, for as long as he remained assistant commander, he never forwarded a single regular report. I'm talking about those reports that he was bound to forward on a daily basis. To put it in simple terms, he was even hostile to certain officers of the JNA. But as he was especially hostile to me, and perhaps that was due to the position that I held during that period, but also later, whenever we met during the war. Instead of greeting me whenever we met, he would always invariably say: "Well, Maso, are you still alive?" That's how he would greet me. Due to all this lack of cooperation, and not because of the way he treated me personally, but because of his lack of cooperation on intelligence and security issues, I spoke to Commander Nikolic and pleaded with Commander Nikolic. I filed a request for Stevan Todorovic's removal from this position, from his position as assistant commander for intelligence and security. However, he was not removed from that position, not because someone was protecting him, but rather because Stevan Todorovic walked out on the JNA, as simple as that, soon after that. And all the events started in Samac municipality and in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Todorovic leave the JNA of his own free will?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, of his own free will. He did not leave with the consent of the JNA. We didn't even know that he had left. The commander never approved him leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll speak about a different subject now. We'll speak about all the illegal weapons, the obtaining of the illegal weapons. As assistant commander for intelligence and security, did you have any personal information or knowledge concerning the illegal obtaining of weapons in the municipalities comprised by the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have this information when I was the assistant commander for intelligence and security of the 17th Tactical Group. I had information that throughout Bosnia, throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, people were being illegally armed, but especially as concerns our zone or area of responsibility, I have information on the municipalities comprised by the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group. People were being armed illegally along the ethnic and party, political lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obtained this information from our Superior Command, as far as weapons in Bosnia and Herzegovina are concerned. And as concerned the existence of illegal weapons and people being illegally armed in our own area of responsibility, our people on the ground and our commanders [as interpreted] for security and intelligence provided this information. But we did have other sources too across the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There is just one word missing here on page 19, line 10. Assistant commanders. The word "assistant" is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information concerning the routes and roads down which the illegal weapons were being brought into Bosnia and Herzegovina, or illegal equipment, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have that kind of information, and the information was that weapons were brought into Bosnia and Herzegovina en masse, over the bridge over the river Sava near Bosanski Samac, and these weapons would usually head for Gradacac, Orasje, and Modrica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had obtained this information, what did the command of the 17th Tactical Group do to prevent this illegal import of weapons and equipment?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following an agreement reached and signed between General Vasiljevic, chief for intelligence and security of the JNA, and Alija Delimustafic, minister of the interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, an agreement in which they agreed to prevent the import of illegal weapons into Bosnia and Herzegovina jointly and to set up joint checkpoints and patrols, jointly between the civilian police and the military police. It was on the basis of this agreement that Commander Nikolic asked for a meeting to be scheduled with the police representatives in Bosanski Samac. Commander Nikolic and I went to the meeting. We attended the meeting. On behalf the police, there was Chief Vinko Dragicevic, there was Dragan Lukac. There were other people there on behalf of the police whom I didn't know, and I still don't know what their names were. On behalf of the JNA there was Commander Nikolic and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any agreement reached? Was any joint, common checkpoint set up?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no agreement was reached. We told them that we were in possession of certain information and knowledge that weapons were being illegally imported over the bridge into Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Republic of Croatia, and we demanded that since the police were already at the bridge, the military police join them. That in itself would be a checkpoint resulting from the intended agreement. However, the police representatives lied to us, by saying that they had everything under control, that there were no illegal weapons coming in, that no illegal weapons were coming into Bosnia over that bridge, that the police were fully in control, and that they themselves had no such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. There was this failure to agree on joint checkpoints. What did the command of the 17th Tactical Group do after that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the failure of the meeting with the police representatives in Bosanski Samac, since we had reliable information that weapons were indeed being brought into Bosnia over that bridge, we were advised by our Superior Command and received their approval. The 17th Tactical Group set up a military checkpoint, military checkpoints in the village of Crkvina and the village of Kornica. Those were roads heading towards Gradacac. However, it was impossible to set up checkpoints there immediately, because those were predominantly Croat villages there. We tried to avoid escalation of the conflict, because the interethnic situation was very bad as it was at that point. So we did not set up a checkpoint on the road to Orasje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It is something that I heard the witness say, and here on page 21, line 10: However, it is impossible to set up checkpoints there immediately because there were predominantly Croat villages there. He was referring to a third checkpoint, not this first villages that he mentioned, Crkvina and Kornica. He was talking about checkpoint towards Orasje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that can be clarified by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the third checkpoint towards Orasje, that that was not set up. Could you please tell us why you didn't set up this third checkpoint towards Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third checkpoint was not set up, the one in the direction of Orasje, so on the road Samac-Orasje, because this road from Samac was already more or less populated exclusively by the Croats. So the setting up of a military checkpoint would further damage the already damaged interethnic relations and would cause even more hostility towards the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was at these checkpoints, and who carried out the controls?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The checkpoints which were set up by the command of the 17th Tactical Group were manned by the military police, from the military police company, which was part of the 17th Tactical Group. Each military police officer at the checkpoint had insignia of his membership of the military police, and he had white belts indicating that he was a member of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Sorry to interrupt. Could we just have some clarification? There's a lot of discussions on checkpoints and the meeting that they held at the SUP, and I thought there was going to be some sort of time period that these incidents occurred, since there's been other testimony, just to see if it's corroborated or if these are different situations that have occurred. So if we could have some time period for the checkpoints, for these meetings and things, I think it would be helpful for all concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is clear with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. I think that I already told the witness that we are still dealing with late 1991 and up to April 1992, so probably we understood one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us: When did this take place? What was the time period? Which year?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military checkpoints and the joint checkpoints which we tried to organise with the police in Bosanski Samac was something that happened in the spring of 1992, i.e., in late May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In late March 1992. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the authority of the military police officers who were at the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police officers who were at these two checkpoints were authorised to stop all suspicious vehicles, to search the contents of those vehicles, regardless of whether it was a passenger vehicle, a freight vehicle, or a bus. That was their task. They were not permitted to check any other documents, such as a driver's licence and whether the car had all the technical equipment as required by law. They could identify or ask for the identification only of suspicious persons in whose possession they found illegal items.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the policemen do when, in the course of their search, they found weapons and military equipment?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If military equipment was found in a vehicle, and it was found - there were such cases - the military police officer was obliged to issue a certificate about the temporary confiscation of such items, whether this was a weapon or ammunition or any other military equipment which should not be in the possession of a civilian. After that, he would make a report, which would be sent to me, as the chief for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you were in the position to see these reports which were sent to you, could you please tell the Trial Chamber about the kinds of items that were confiscated at these checkpoints, "items" meaning military equipment and so on. What were the items confiscated by those police officers?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the military checkpoints were set up, we immediately confirmed our information that illegal weapons were being brought in in these roads, illegal military equipment and ammunition. All kinds of things were found, not just artillery weapons. The items that were most frequently found were automatic rifles whose origin was the Yugoslav People's Army. A lot of automatic rifles of Chinese manufacture were also found. They were probably obtained in the markets in the Republic of Croatia. A lot of explosives were found, also a lot of hand grenades, ammunition, as well as other military equipment, meaning binoculars, in the colours of the Yugoslav People's Army. So it meant that this was something that was not for sale. Also there were some protective masks and pieces of uniforms and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened, if you know, after a few days, a few days after the checkpoint was set up in Crkvina, where the military police were? Were there any changes or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not right away, but perhaps seven or eight days after the checkpoints were set up, the military checkpoints, the police from Samac now asked the representatives of our command, our commander, to -- so for them to be allowed to have civilian police officers man these checkpoints as well. After this request, and in accordance with the agreement that was reached and signed, the commander did not grant it. I don't want to say that, but he accepted that, and he ordered or he informed me and the military police that in future, the civilian police would also be present at the checkpoint. It was now said that the civilian police will carry out duties from their domain. They would stop passengers, check their identification, search the vehicles, and that the military police would continue to perform the duties that it was performing until that time. It was said that the civilian police would be stopping the vehicles, and not the military police. However, if at the request of a military policeman, the civilian police officer did not wish to stop a certain vehicle, the military police officer did have the right to stop that suspicious vehicle and to conduct the search.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you properly, these were then joint checkpoints, manned by the civilian and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were then joint, or mixed checkpoints after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the checks that were conducted at the checkpoint, how long did they last? I'm thinking of how long did they last during the day.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were maintained around the clock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, do you have any information or knowledge about the illegal arming and military organising of Muslims in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have knowledge about that, that the Muslim population in Samac, the town of Samac, because that's where they were in the municipality, that's where they were living, that they were organising themselves in a military sense, that they had military units formed, that these units had their commanders with areas of responsibility, and that those units were also active according to the principle of subordination, just like any army in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could that be clarified? Number one, could he indicate the source of his information? Is this just information passed up or is this information that he obtained working in an undercover capacity which would therefore be based on his personal knowledge? Also, when he says "Muslim population," is he including every Muslim? Is he including Mr. Zaric's wife? Was she part of an illegal military? Could he just clarify that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pisarevic, I'm sure, will deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We will clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you obtain this information about the forming and military organising of Muslims in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information about the organising of Muslims in Bosanski Samac was something that we obtained from our associates, from people who lived in Bosanski Samac, who knew something about that. And later, it turned out that this information was true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have information about who led this military organisation and who led this arming of the members of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had knowledge about that as well. We received information about them organising militarily, and in the same way we found out that they organised themselves with the help and with cooperation of the Party for Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Simeunovic, you mentioned that you got the information about the organising of Muslims in Bosanski Samac from your associates, from people who lived in Bosanski Samac. Was one of these associates Mr. Zaric, and was this one of the tasks that you mention that he performed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. His task, Simo Zaric's task as assistant commander for intelligence and security, was also to gather such information about illegal arming, about the forming of paramilitary formations of the Yugoslav People's Army. That was his task, his main task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if that was his main task, what were his other tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were other tasks as well. The basic task was to preserve the existing order which was in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the main task of all of us. He had other tasks as well stemming from that, for example, about the sabotage that was being carried out, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, there is something here in the answer of the witness that maybe -- I don't think it needs any clarification. It's just -- in page 27, he was talking about gathering informations about forming of paramilitary formations. Here it says of Yugoslav People's Army. This is something that the witness didn't say, so if it could be taken out of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe he can be taken back to repeat what he said, so we have a correct report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier those paramilitary units or organisations. What are these paramilitary units, according to your understanding of that particular category?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "paramilitary formations" to me means all those units which are militarily structured but are not under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army, but have their own tasks which are even -- not even, but they are quite contrary to the tasks of the Yugoslav People's Army, because if they were the same, then they would comprise one army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have information that armed and militarily organised members of the Muslim people, under the patronage of the SDA, have their own checkpoints and patrols in the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object, Your Honour. It's a very leading question. His only answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll modify my question. No problem. I'll change the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information concerning the activities of militarily structured units of Muslims and the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have such information. Personally, I noticed these things. Whenever I went with the commander to a meeting, or whenever we came to the detachment command, the vehicle would always be followed. We were being tailed by civilians patrolling the town. They always knew about the route our vehicle would take.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any information concerning the illegal arming and military organising of the Croatian population in Bosanski Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had that kind of information too, yes. We also had information that the Croatian people -- when I say "the Croatian people," I'm referring to men of military age and men who were fit for military service. I'm just trying to avoid the issue that we had before, whether a woman was taking part in some operations. So again, I say I'm referring to men of military age. We did have such information, information that the Croats too were organising themselves in the military sense, that they had set up their own military units, and these units had their commanders, their areas of responsibility. Like all the armies of the world, they were functioning according to the principle of subordination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information about the presence of military instructors training soldiers, training soldiers coming from the Republic of Croatia and from the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew about that too. We knew that instructors were coming to train these units that had been set up, units, military units, set up along the party and ethnic lines. Mostly instructors were coming for the Croatian units that had been set up, and those instructors were mostly arriving from the Republic of Croatia. Those were people from the territories of municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina who would sometimes go to Croatia to be trained and then they would return there to, in their turn, train other soldiers and other units and sometimes they were in command of these units. We did have such information. We also knew that instructors from Sarajevo were coming to train soldiers and that the whole thing had been organised by the SDA. All this information was later proven correct, because during military operations in early 1992, we captured a number of HVO members who had been trained in the Republic of Croatia, who were carrying on them an ID saying "military instructor," a military instructor fully equipped to train and command lower-ranking units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information concerning the presence of members of Croatia's National Guard in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew about that. Members of the National Guard were spending time in the Samac municipal area, and particularly in Orasje municipality. When I say this, I say it because I actually saw these members of the National Guard. I saw them manning a checkpoint in the village of Grebnice in Bosanski Samac municipality. I was stopped at that checkpoint by them. I was wearing civilian clothes. This was sometime in March, in early March 1992, I believe. They were wearing uniform and insignia of the National Guard, and there were armed civilians with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who does this National Guard belong to, this military unit?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military unit referred to as the National Guard belongs to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, do you know anything about the arming of Serbs in the area of responsibility, or the way they were organising themselves militarily in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew about that too. Serbs, much like Muslims and Croats, were obtaining illegal weapons and were organising themselves militarily in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If we're speaking about the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group, as far as the illegal arming of Serbs is concerned, we knew that there were individual cases of Serbs obtaining weapons illegally, but we have no information to the effect that there was an organised military unit, a paramilitary unit organised by Serbs. We did not have any such information, because the Serbs had responded to the mobilisation call-up and they were members of units of the Yugoslav People's Army, whereas the other ethnic groups followed the instructions, so to speak, and requests of their own respective leaders: Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that later on. Did you have any information concerning the republic-level Bosnia-Herzegovina? Were Serbs organising themselves into military units? And how did you obtain such information, if any?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have such information, and we would receive our information from superior commands. We would review the information and analyse this information. If you look at the area of responsibility of the 17th Corps, part of which was also the 17th Tactical Group, Serbs obtained weapons, armed themselves, in those towns, in those municipalities where the army was not present, in those localities where Serb communities were isolated from the JNA, wherever the JNA was not around and Serbs had no mobilisation call-ups to respond to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this would be a convenient time to break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take our break and continue our proceedings at 1715 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Makso, when you spoke about the units within the 17 Tactical Group of the JNA, you referred to the armoured battalion. Can you tell me, please: What was the ethnic structure of the armoured battalion when the battalion was mobilised in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ethnic structure, make-up, of the 2nd Armoured Battalion of the 395th Motorised Brigade was mixed. It included Croats, Serbs, and Muslims. Commanders were also of mixed ethnicity. In addition to Serb commanders, there were Croat and Muslim commanders too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the ethnic make-up of the battalion remain the same in the course of 1992? I'm referring to the ethnic structure of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't remain the same. Immediately after the setting up, after the mobilisation in October, after between 10 and 15 days, the ethnic make-up of the battalion began to change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way did the ethnic make-up of the battalion start changing? What started happening?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following the instructions of the party leaders, Franjo Tudjman of the HDZ and Alija Izetbegovic of the SDA, those members who had responded to the mobilisation call-up started deserting, started abandoning JNA units, so that eventually, at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, in the battalion there were no conscripts of any other ethnic groups apart from Serb conscripts, whereas the professional soldiers, the commissioned officers, remained until mid-April 1992, when they too left the armoured battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As you were the assistant commander for intelligence and security, you and your own commander, did you report to your superior command on these phenomena?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did send reports. It was our obligation to send these reports, to forward these reports to our superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your superior command, was there any feedback from your superior command as to how and whether they acted on your reports?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not receive any feedback from our superior command as to whether and how they acted on our reports, but it wasn't their obligation to inform me, because I was inferior in rank to them. But we had received instructions, so to speak, because the conscripts who had deserted from the JNA were under the authority of military bodies, so they were under the military police, not the civilian police. The military police. We had received instructions not to bring these conscripts into the military units because they were living in towns and villages where Serbs didn't live. Those were predominantly Croat and Muslims villages. So such action on our part would have caused the gap to deepen between the people, on the one hand, and the JNA on the other. So we followed the instructions received and we didn't force anyone back into the military units. But if you would please allow me, I would like to give you a specific case about a conscript who I believe did not desert from the JNA. This conscript was born in Gradacac, and when he was on leave and when he returned from his leave, towards the end of 1991, he spoke to his commander, Milorad Zivanovic, and he told him: "I'm not sure what to do, Mile. There's a lot of pressure on my family. My family is being mistreated because I am a member of the JNA. I don't know what to do." The major then told him: "If that's what the situation is like" - and he knew what the overall situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was like at that time - he simply told him: "You're free to walk." He told him he was free to leave the Yugoslav People's Army. He thanked him and told him that he thought the situation would quieten down soon enough for him to return to his unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But just by way of clarification: You referred to Gradacac and to this conscript. What was his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gradacac, the town which the conscript hailed from, what is the ethnic make-up of Gradacac predominantly?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gradacac is predominantly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said before that in the 17th Tactical Group there was a military police company too. Can you now please tell us something about this military police company and its tasks? Was that a special unit within the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a military police company. They had their own commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had the authority to issue orders to this military police company?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the military police company would receive orders from the commander of the Tactical Group, or from the Chief of Staff in the commander's absence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the procedure for the engagement of military police should detachment commands require their engagement?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A request would come from any of the detachments for military police to be engaged, and the commander would then order me - that was actually part of my duties - to make an assessment of how many forces, how many military police officers were to be engaged. I'd forward my proposal back to the commander and then he would issue an order for a certain section of the military police to be engaged on a specific task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was the managing of weapons controlled, those weapons that members of the detachment, of the 17th Tactical Group, were in charge of?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons that members of the 17th Tactical Group from the detachment were in charge of, those weapons were kept at their homes. So no control was carried out by the police. They didn't go into people's houses to see where these weapons were being kept. The police didn't do this, the military police. If there was any self -- if there was any wilful use of these weapons and were such cases occurred, people heard about it, then the detachment commander would file a request for the military police to step in, and then the military police would go and see this person who had been accused of wilful use of weapons, or irregular use of weapons. But if this person merely carried the weapons about town, this would have required sanctions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the detachment commanders could not engage on their own initiative the military police?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they couldn't just pick up the phone and say: "We need three or five police officers". They had to go through the proper channels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any examples of the command of the 4th Detachment to report their members because of the inadequate use and handling of weapons by members of the detachment?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such cases did occur, and I know that the command of the 4th Detachment requested that some members of the detachment who wilfully used weapons, who fired them, be disarmed by the military police, and this was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I just wish to say that this was also done in other detachments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the case of the checkpoint at Grebnice when personal weapons were taken away from active military personnel? Do you know anything about that event? And if you do, could you please briefly tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about this event. At that time I was the chief for intelligence and security in the 17th Tactical Group. Two active officers, members of the command of the 17th Tactical Group, had their weapons taken away from them at the Grebnice checkpoint, even though they had regular permits signed by Commander Nikolic for those weapons. The weapons were confiscated by members of the National Guard of the Republic of Croatia, and this happened at the same checkpoint where I was asked for my ID previously. I can't say if they were the same persons as the ones who confiscated the weapons, but they also had uniforms. They were wearing uniforms of the National Guard. When this happened, they returned to the command of the 17th Tactical Group. They informed the commander about what happened. The commander was very angry because someone, and particularly it being the army coming from a different state to disarm officers of the JNA, because this village is in the municipality of Samac, he immediately went to the police station. He also told me to go with him, so I did go with him. We came to the police station. He asked to see Chief Dragicevic, who, however, was not at the station at the time, and we were received by Vinko. We talked to him. The commander actually talked with Lukac, Dragan Lukac. I said Vinko earlier, but it was Dragan Lukac. He was very angry while conducting this conversation, and he told him that he will not tolerate any more such acts, whereby officers of the JNA were being disarmed, particularly officers and active military personnel. Dragan Lukac tried to calm down the commander, and he said that he would see why this happened. We were told to come back tomorrow to the police station and that he would take steps to return these weapons to the police station. The next day, the commander did not go. He sent me instead. I came to the station. I went to see Lukac and he returned these weapons. Previously he told the commander that he will conduct an investigation, establish what happened, and then the commander would be informed about what was done, but the commander actually never received any report indicating anything that was done in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with events regarding the setting up of barricades at the entrances to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that incident. This happened in early April. I don't know the exact date, but approximately on the 10th or the 11th of April, when the military police patrolled the area of responsibility, and while doing this, they came up -- they met armed civilians. They had military weapons, automatic weapons, which, according to any regulations, they were not permitted to have. The military police disarmed these civilians, brought the weapons to the 17th Tactical Group. They made a report about this, and in the morning they informed me about what they did, or actually what happened while they were out performing their tasks. After that, we received information that barricades had been erected in the town of Samac, that it was not possible to enter Samac or to leave it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive information about who erected those barricades?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive this information, i.e., that the barricades were erected by the citizens of Samac, Muslim citizens, led by the Party for Democratic Action, because the persons who had been disarmed the previous evening were actually a patrol which was formed by the Party for Democratic Action, and that was one of those separate units that I talked about a little earlier when I was saying how the commander and I were followed any time we entered Samac. So those were actually the patrols that tailed us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone call the command from Samac by telephone?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning, right after the disarming and the erecting of the barricades, Izet Izetbegovic called the 17th Tactical Group. He asked to speak to Commander Nikolic. However, Commander Nikolic was not at the command. He was in Brcko. So he talked with Major Brajkovic, the chief of the tactical group, and I know that the chief told him to call Commander Nikolic in Brcko to find him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you know about that? Did Mr. Izetbegovic speak with Mr. Nikolic? Did Mr. Nikolic tell you anything about that afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after this call from Samac, this call by Izetbegovic, Major Brajkovic called the commander by telephone in Brcko, informed him about what happened in Samac and that he would -- and told him that Izet Izetbegovic would call him. The commander ordered, or told Brajkovic, that the army should not be used for this purpose, that no order should be issued for the use of the army. When the commander returned from Brcko - this was sometime around noon - those of us who were at the command were told that he had talked with Izetbegovic, that Izetbegovic had called him in Brcko, and he said that he begged him not to use the army regarding these barricades, that they would resolve that, that he would make sure that they were taken -- that they were dismantled. And then the commander promised that he would not use the army, that he didn't have any intention of using the army, because that was not one of the purposes of the army. It was not one of the army's tasks. This was something that would be done by the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, whether there were any sabotages or diversions in the territory of Bosanski Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were aware of that. We received information about that. This was something that we were informed about by the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the 4th Detachment, Simo Zaric, that there had been some sabotage acts, several of them, that there were casualties in the cafes. The sabotage acts involved transmission lines, the chapel at the Orthodox cemetery was blown up. We were informed about all of the acts of sabotage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conduct any investigations to find out the perpetrators of those sabotage acts?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We, as the army, as the JNA, did not take any steps regarding those sabotage acts. We just passed on the reports to the Superior Command, but we did not take any steps, because this was in the jurisdiction of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to move to another event now. What do you know about the arrival of volunteers to the village of Batkusa? Could you please tell the Trial Chamber about that.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual arrival is something that I know everything about. On the 11th of April, sometime in the morning, an associate of mine called me and he told me: "Makso, guests are coming to you, to Batkusa." When he said guests are arriving, I understood him to mean that these were not guests who were personally coming to visit me. Had they been such, they would come directly to me, to the command post. And then he said: "If you want to find out who is coming, then you should go there." After this conversation with him, I called the commander. The commander was in a meeting with some people. I apologised and I just said: "Commander, I need to go to see the 1st Detachment." Without interrupting the meeting, he indicated with his hand that I could go, so I went to Batkusa. I went to the command post. I don't know where else I was supposed to go. I wasn't told where to go, where these guests would be arriving. I went to the command of the 1st Detachment in Batkusa. It was on the premises of the local community, in the centre of the village. In front of it, as I was arriving, I could see in front of the command the commander of the detachment, Mico Ivanovic, aka Mijak. Stevan Todorovic was also with him. There was also a group of villagers there, a small group of villagers from Batkusa. I think they were from Batkusa. Civilians. And I arrived in an official vehicle. When I came out of the vehicle and walked towards Commander Mijak, Stevan Todorovic turned, and when he saw me, he was very surprised. I would like to say right away that this was the first time that I saw Stevan Todorovic at the detachment command. I came there many times, but I never saw him at the command. He was very surprised when he saw me, and instead of greeting me, he asked me: "What are you doing here, Makso? Why did you come?" I came up to the commander. I greeted him, to Mijak. And then I responded to Stevan: "I'm here. I've come to the detachment command." And we stood about there for a little bit longer. I didn't speak with Stevan. I talked to Mijak and I asked him: "What is happening?" I could see that something was going on there. And having had this information about the arrival of guests, I asked him: "What is going on?" And he just shrugged. He didn't say anything. As we were talking, you could hear the sound of a helicopter from the direction of Brcko. At this sound, the villagers who were there, as well as Stevan Todorovic, as well as Mijak and myself, went to the football field which was right behind the premises of the command. As we were going there, we could see the helicopter approaching, one helicopter, and it landed on the football field. I could see that it had insignia of the Yugoslav People's Army. And the helicopter didn't even touch the ground yet. Even before it touched down, people, soldiers in camouflage uniforms, jumped out. They had paint on their faces. They were carrying weapons and running. They took up defensive positions around the chopper, which hadn't touched down yet. They took up defensive positions, stood still, and pointed the weapons towards us, even though we were standing outside of the football field. I was confused at first. My first thought was that it was a military exercise or something. But the information about the arrival of guests -- and I was quite confused about what was going on. Immediately after they jumped out of the helicopter and took up the defensive positions, the helicopter touched down. After that, you could hear the sound of another helicopter. The helicopter also came and landed on the field, not in the same way as this one. It touched down all the way, and uniformed soldiers came out of that helicopter also. They too had paint on their faces. Some of them were wearing those hats. We call them cowboy hats. And some of them also had caps. They didn't take up a defensive or a combat position. As they were coming out, they formed a group. Three men separated off from the group. They were in uniforms with painted faces, and they started walking towards us. Commander Mijak and I stood a little way away from Todorovic, maybe three or four metres away from him, and they actually were walking straight towards Stevan Todorovic, and they greeted him, based on which I concluded that they knew each other from before, that this was not the first time that they met, because they greeted one another cordially. After a brief conversation there - How did you travel? How was your trip? Is everything all right? That was the substance of the conversation - Stevan Todorovic led them towards the command building. We also, Commander Mijak and myself, followed them. We followed Stevan and those other three people. And then I noticed, when we started walking, that those soldiers who had taken up the combat positions were not in that position any more and that the villagers were approaching the soldiers. We entered the command, Stevan and the three of them who arrived entered first. I didn't know who those people were, but now I do. They were Djordjevic -- you see how the name suddenly comes to you. I can't remember the first time, but his nickname was Crni. There was also Srecko Radovanovic, also known as Debeli, the fat one. And there was Lugar, Slobodan Miljkovic, nicknamed Lugar, the wood-keeper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't the name of this person called Djordjevic Dragan by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Dragan Djordjevic. I've just remembered. They entered the command building. The commander and I followed. No one was really paying any attention to us. The conversation was between Stevan Todorovic and the three men who came. They sat down, talked briefly. Stevan told them that everything had been taken care of, or prepared, that accommodation would be provided in the village of Obudovac. That's the neighbouring village. That accommodation would be provided at the football stadium in Obudovac. Then they set out for Obudovac. They were walking in a combat disposition on their way to Obudovac. Both sides of the roads there were columns marching, one by one, with their weapons pointed at villagers who were in their front yards watching. It was a simple demonstration of power. Those who were walking at the back of the column would occasionally look over their shoulders. So this was how they went to Obudovac.
