utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having seen that, what steps did you take?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having seen all of that, I waited for them to walk away, and then I headed straight back to the command building. I wanted to tell the commander about this situation which took place. Had this been announced, I would have known myself, being a member of the command, that they would be arriving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say the commander. Can you please state his full name? Which command, which place?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to the command of the 17th Tactical Group, and I reported about what I had seen happening in the area of responsibility of the 1st Detachment in Obudovac. I told Stevan Milinkovic [as interpreted], who was the commander of the 17th Tactical Group. He was very surprised by what I told him. At first he couldn't believe that I was telling the truth. How would that have been possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one short correction on page 45, line 1. Stevan Nikolic, not Milinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can -- that's the correct name, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Nikolic, as I've said, was taken aback. He couldn't believe that anything like that was possible without him knowing. He immediately phoned the Superior Command to check, to see, to ask them what was going on and who had arrived and what the reason was. I was in the office when he made the call. I didn't hear what the feedback was from the Superior Command, but what I could glean from what Commander Nikolic told them and from his answers to their questions, I concluded that they had no idea what was going on exactly. My impression was that he received a task from the Superior Command to look into the matter to find out who those people were, why they had come and what their mission was, and to inform him of all these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please just tell us what the Superior Command was, the Superior Command of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Superior Command of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA was the 17th Corps, with command post in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commander was who?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Sava Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What did Commander Nikolic do after that? What steps did he take after he had talked to his Superior Command?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After he talked to the Superior Command, Commander Nikolic kept on making phone calls. I think he was probably putting calls through to Samac. And he said that they had agreed that the next day there would be a meeting with the representatives in Donji Zabar that there would be a meeting in Donji Zabar with the representatives of the civilian authorities, or with someone in Samac, that is, in Donji Zabar. I don't know exactly who they were supposed to be meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the meeting eventually held in Donji Zabar?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The next day, a meeting took place in Donji Zabar. I did not attend this meeting. Commander Stevan Nikolic was representing the command at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Following that meeting, did Commander Nikolic tell you what had been happening at the meeting in Donji Zabar, or what had been discussed at the meeting and what agreements had been reached? If so, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon his return from the meeting in Donji Zabar, Commander Nikolic informed us at the command of the 17th Tactical Group that a meeting -- that the meeting had been held, that the meeting had been attended by the three men who had arrived by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us their first and last names?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Djordjevic, nicknamed Crni; Srecko Radovanovic, nicknamed Debeli; and Slobodan Miljkovic, nicknamed Lugar. They attended the meeting. That's what Commander Nikolic told us. Stevan Todorovic was also there. He said that at the meeting, when he brought up the question as to who the people were who had arrived by helicopter and why they had arrived, he was told that those were members of the Serb militia of Serbian Krajina, that they had official papers, official IDs, testifying to the fact that they were members of the Serbian police force of Serbian Krajina. And then he told us that in addition to the first group that had arrived, another group was being sent over, a group that was part of mostly the 1st Detachment, but also included people from other detachments, a group including about 23, I think, young volunteers who had been sent over for training. They were supposed to go to a training camp in Sarengrad. The group was led by Aca Jankovic, a person born in Batkusa. At this meeting, Commander Nikolic was also told that the army had no authority to give orders to members of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, which was true, and Commander Nikolic was fully aware of that. But since they had arrived in the area of responsibility commanded by him personally, he merely wanted to know the reasons for their arrival, what their intentions were, what they were about to do, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Commander Nikolic, commander of the 17th Tactical Group, informed his Superior Command about this meeting, the conclusions reached at the meeting, and what he learned there?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did report to the Superior Command. He conveyed to them what had been said at the meeting. He informed them that those were not members of the JNA but, rather, members of the MUP, that those were members of the MUP of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please: Do you know where Sarengrad is located exactly?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that. Sarengrad is near Ilok. That's in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which of the authorities -- who held that part of Croatia, that territory where Sarengrad and Ilok are, at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarengrad and Ilok, that area was under the authority of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Following that, the 17th Tactical Group, did they take any measures concerning checks, controls, in relation to these newly arrived volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was our task. We tried to find out the reason why they had arrived, the group arriving in our area of responsibility. However, just like we were not able to find out in time that a group had been sent over, the group of our own units, for training, to Sarengrad, we were not able to find out the reasons for the arrival of this group, at least initially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we shall discuss events which started happening on the 16th of April, 1992. Do you recall that night, the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992? Where were you on that night?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before you answer that question, I want to go back to your answer starting on page 48, line 12. The last three words after the comma: "At least initially." What are you hinting at by saying "at least initially"? You said: "We were not able to find out the reasons for the arrival of this group, at least initially." What are you, so to say, meaning by those words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that, when I used the word "initially," what I meant is just what I was about to include in my next answer, because eventually we did find out the reasons for the arrival of that group. But between the 11th and the 16th, we were trying to get at the reasons behind their arrival, but we could not succeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us: Do you remember the day between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992, and where were you on that night?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, the night between the 16th and the 17th, I do recall that night. I was at the command of the 17th Tactical Group. I was sleeping. I was resting that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in the village of Pelagicevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, in Pelagicevo. The rooms we used for rest were on the first floor of the command building. It was a rather large private house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us with any degree of accuracy: What is the distance between Pelagicevo and Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distance between Pelagicevo and Bosanski Samac is between 25 and 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find out that night? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, about 3.00 in the morning on the 17th, the duty officer from the 17th Tactical Group woke us up, myself and others, the officers who were there, the officers who were sleeping at the command building. He said that the commander was looking for us and wanted us to go down to the command hall immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, very quickly. We slept on the first floor. We just put on some clothes and went straight down to see him. The commander was already in the command hall at his table. Once we assembled, and we didn't take that long, as I said, the commander told us that Blagoje Simic, from Samac, had called him, telling him that the volunteers who had arrived, the group of volunteers, had taken facilities and buildings of vital importance in the town of Samac, and that the civilian police forces, alongside with them, took part in the taking of those vital buildings and institutions in the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Commander Nikolic tell you anything else on that occasion about what the command would do and so on?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this brief information about the current situation in Samac, Commander Nikolic ordered that all detachments raise their combat readiness to a higher level. Also, he called by telephone for the commander of the 4th Detachment, Radovan Antic, and the assistant commander for intelligence and security, Simo Zaric, to come to the command of the 17th Tactical Group in Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when Mr. Antic, as the commander, and Mr. Zaric, came to Pelagicevo? And if you can recall, could you please tell us what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there, but, in view of the situation, that was normal, because that's where the command was all the time. Commander Antic and Simo Zaric came in the morning hours. I think it was sometime between 5.00 and 6.00 a.m. I don't know exactly what time it was, but it was between 5.00 and 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Commander Nikolic tell them at that point?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Radovan Antic and Simo Zaric arrived at the command, Nikolic explained to them briefly what happened. He asked them whether they knew anything about what was happening. They just said that on their way there, they saw those members of the special forces. They had these uniforms and their faces were painted. They were all over town, and that they didn't know what was going on. When the commander briefly told them what he told us in the command when we came, then he ordered that upon return to the command post, the 4th Detachment should be called up, but nothing should be undertaken without his order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than raising the state of alert to a high level in the detachments, did the 17th Tactical Group conduct any other consultations or do anything with the Superior Command? What were actually the activities that were conducted that morning?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after finding out what was happening in the town of Samac, Commander Nikolic informed the Superior Command, i.e., the 17th Corps in Tuzla. He informed them about what happened in the town of Samac and in the municipality of Samac, and he asked for instructions. I say "instructions," even though he knew what his tasks were. But he requested additional instructions about what to do in the situation as it was at that time. And he said that he received orders from the Superior Command that the units of the Yugoslav People's Army should not be used, that the combat readiness level should be raised, but only the 4th Detachment should be called, because all of this was going on in the area of responsibility of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information about the changes that had taken place in Samac? What happened in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have information that there was a takeover of power. This is what Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic told us, that power in Samac and in the municipality of Samac had switched hands and that now it was the Serbian municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any intelligence data or information about any activities of other organised paramilitary units or military units?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information right after when Commander Nikolic and Simo Zaric came, Commander Antic. They didn't stay in the command for a long time. They perhaps stayed for half an hour. Immediately after that, they went to the command post of the 4th Detachment in Samac. Before leaving, Commander Antic telephoned the command of the 4th Detachment and ordered the call-up. So he carried out the tasks that were supposed to be carried out before the commander arrived. After they left, after a certain period of time, already in the morning of the 17th of April, we had some information about the events in the actual town of Samac, as well as the events in the surrounding villages around Samac. We had information that other than the police, which had already taken the vital facilities, as well as the volunteers from the Serbian Krajina, the militia of the Serbian Krajina, that also a large group of armed civilians had appeared. Since everybody knows everybody in the town of Samac - it's a small town - everybody knew that they were Muslims. They organised themselves, let me put it that way. I had already talked about those units. Those units had already been formed and were already out on the streets. They were smaller groups, but if you actually counted them, they numbered about 100 armed people, armed men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Did Commander Nikolic on that day, the 17th of April, 1992, issue any orders to the command of the 4th Detachment, if you know? And if you know, could you please tell us what these orders were.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Commander Nikolic did issue tasks to the 4th Detachment, to the commander of the 4th Detachment. Based on this information which we received, and information that already on the left bank of the river Sava, as well as the left bank of the river Bosna, movements were seen by some units, the commander issued a task to the commander of the 4th Detachment to take a number of the men and to go to the right bank of the Bosna River, towards the village of Prud, in the municipality of Odzak, and also to go to the right bank of the river Sava, facing the Republic of Croatia. This order was issued sometime around noon or in the early afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Commander Nikolic at that point also issued an order about the collection of illegal weapons in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. He issued that order to the commander of the 4th Detachment. Having received information about illegal arming in Samac, and that civilians had military weapons, automatic weapons, Commander Nikolic gave the commander of the 4th Detachment, Radovan Nikolic [as interpreted], the task of taking the men which were left over after the detachment was deployed to the two positions, towards the Republic of Croatia and the village of Prud. So that they could go and collect the illegal weapons. At that point he ordered them not to enter into houses or conduct searches of those houses, but to conduct this collection of weapons on a voluntary basis, to call the citizens and ask them to bring out their weapons and to surrender them, or if they did not wish to be seen as people who were handing over the weapons, they could just leave them in front of their houses, outside their houses, and that the members of the 4th Detachment would collect them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the following event: That Ibrahim Salkic, on the telephone, spoke with Commander Nikolic on the 17th of April? Do you have any information about that, personal information or knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there when he talked with him, but Commander Nikolic said - because I was in and out of the command building - that he had received a call from Ibrahim Salkic and that he had told him on the telephone that he was with a large group of armed people and that he didn't know what to do. This is what Commander Nikolic said, that he was simply asking the commander for advice about what to do. So he told him that he should not use weapons in any event, that they should hand over the weapons to the members of the 4th Detachment. I think that that is what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive regular reports from the 4th Detachment command, the Tactical Group command, and did you continue to receive reports from Mr. Zaric about what was going on in Samac, whether the command orders were being carried out and so on? Could you please tell us a little bit about how all of this functioned.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive those reports. I received reports from Simo Zaric, regularly. When I say "regularly," I mean that it was continuous. It wasn't: "I will report at such-and-such a point." But as he received information about the events in Samac, using the means available to him, he would forward these reports to the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember receiving any information about how these Sareni, and the police who participated in the takeover, actually detained some members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was information to that effect. These volunteers brought in members of the 4th Detachment also to the police station, the 4th Detachment of the JNA. They were not of Serb ethnicity. They were Muslims. Simo Zaric informed us about this in the command, and I know that Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic was very angry because of this. He called Stevan Todorovic on the telephone, because he was already appointed chief of police upon the takeover of power in Samac. So he called Stevan Todorovic and told him that members of the Yugoslav People's Army must not be arrested, that he would send Simo Zaric to the police station to take these people off the hands of the police, so that these people can be released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any other information about events, arrests, and so on, from Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received other information. Simo informed us that he went to the station in relation to this event and that those people were released from the police station. We received information that members of other ethnic groups were being arrested in the town of Samac and that people were being -- there was a kind of extortion involved, where people were being asked for money for the purpose of personal enrichment of those volunteers. They were taking money. That's what we had information about. We also had information that the people who had been brought in were being physically abused. We also received information that some people were arrested about whom we had information that they took part in the illegal arming of the Muslim population - these were people of Muslim ethnicity - that they imported weapons illegally and that they were held at the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and Commander Nikolic, after you received this information, what did you order Simo Zaric to do?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we had received all this information, and particularly the information concerning the arrests of persons who we believed had taken part in the illegal arming, Commander Nikolic ordered Simo Zaric to go to the police station where those persons were being kept, to look at the statements that had been taken, if any, and to talk to whatever persons he saw fit, in connection with the illegal arming. Because there was suspicion that a number of military staff had taken part in the arming. Weapons were also arriving from military warehouses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zaric do that? Did he inform you about that? What information did he obtain?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He kept reporting to us. And before that, the commander had told Stevan Todorovic about Simo Zaric arriving there, that Simo Zaric would look at the statements and, if necessary, conduct further interviews, and that all those persons from whom statements had not been taken would be made to make statements. As far as I know, Simo talked to two or three persons from whom statements had not yet been taken, and he reported back to us on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Just a question for clarification. Which are the time frames for these events you are now talking about? Is it on the 17th of April or the following days? It would be useful to know what are the time frames. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain the events we've just discussed, from the 17th on. Well, of course you may not remember the exact date, but if you could just give us a rough time frame.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these things happened between the 17th, when part of the members of the 7th [as interpreted] Detachment came out. That was on the 17th, in the afternoon hours. The collection of weapons also took place in the afternoon hours on the 17th and continued on the morning of the 18th. The arrests that I was talking about, the arrests being carried out by the volunteers, that took place on the 18th, 19th, and 20th. The taking of statements that I talked about, when Simo Zaric went over to the police station in Samac, that was about two or three days later. It may have been the 18th or the 19th, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Simo Zaric, did he come to the command in Pelagicevo to see you and Commander Nikolic? Did he complain about Stevan Todorovic's actions or about the actions of the volunteers, the members of the special forces or the Sareni, however you choose to refer to them, who had maltreated him at the police station in Samac? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After these events, Simo Zaric used to come quite frequently to the command of the detachment; not every day, but rather often. After this task he had received from Commander Nikolic to go to the police station and to have the statements taken, he told us that what he experienced at the station was unlike anything else he had experienced in his life. He told us that members of the Special Forces, and one man in particular - I can never seem to remember the man's name, but the nickname was Vuk - he mistreated Simo. At one point he even drew his pistol and put the pistol's barrel into Simo's mouth. Simo requested the commander to do something about it, but the commander was trying to talk sense into him and to tell him to calm down, and eventually succeeded, I believe, so that Simo went back to his command, the 4th Detachment, and kept on sending reports to us. While he was at the station, he told us that persons were being mistreated there and that he saw persons being mistreated in passing, and those persons seemed as if they had been beaten black and blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon receiving all this information, were you given any kind of task by Commander Nikolic? And tell us what you know about it. Actually, I'm referring to the transfer of detainees to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about what happened, because I myself took part in it. After we received information from Simo Zaric that some persons had even been killed, some of the detainees, that is, I received a phone call from Captain Momcilo Petrovic, assistant commander for intelligence and security at the Brcko garrison. He told me that Simo had phoned him, both now and earlier. He told me that Simo had informed him about the same things he told us, in a very dramatic tone of voice, as Petrovic said, Simo appealed for help, for those people to be helped in some way. He could not give any suggestions as to what should be done to help those people, but he did plead with Petrovic for those people to be protected, and he was asking us the same thing, the 17th Tactical Group. After that, Captain Petrovic had a talk with Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, and as he later told me, they reached an agreement as to what precisely to do to save those people. They had reached a conclusion that it was best to transfer those people who had been detained in Samac to the barracks in Brcko, where they would be safe and protected. There was no appropriate -- no other appropriate location in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group, and besides, the policemen who were maltreating them were in the area too. Commander Nikolic called me and told me that he had agreed with Captain Petrovic for us to - I think it was on the 26th. That's if I remember correctly. The 26th of April, 1992 - for us -- for me to go to Samac with some of the military police, with vehicles, to pick those people up at the Territorial Defence staff building in Samac, where they were being kept, and from the police station, which is across the road from the staff, and to take those people to Brcko and to hand them over to the military police there and the military garrison in Brcko. Commander Nikolic told me: "Do as you see fit, how many military policemen you need to carry out this task, carry out an assessment, take as many people as you think you need. If you think the whole thing might require more people -- if you think there are not enough people in one platoon, or if the platoon was not filled," he said that I could even take army members with me to carry out this task, people who weren't necessarily military policemen. He also told me to avoid, by all means, conflict with the volunteers, with the Serbian police, but he also did emphasise that I was supposed to complete my mission. He said I should take as many vehicles as I thought were necessary. He said we had between 50 and 60 vehicles there. He didn't know the exact --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. People there, not vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't know the exact number, but that's what he told me. I took the task very seriously, knowing what the volunteers were like and that they would stop at nothing. I took off with three official vehicles. There were 20 military policemen accompanying me. I thought that was as many as I needed. There was a lorry, two Pinzgauers, and my official vehicle. The commander told me, as I was about to set out, that Simo Zaric would be waiting for me in Samac. I set out -- I reached Samac in the late afternoon hours. It was getting dark. Outside the police station and the TO staff was where we stopped. Simo Zaric was waiting for us there. With him was Savo Cancarevic, a police officer; another man who was there was another police officer, Topolovac. I think his name was Mile. When we arrived outside the station, the first thing I did, I handed out tasks to the commander of the military police to secure the area surrounding the police station and the TO staff. Next thing, Simo Zaric came up to me and he seem agitated. He said: "Hurry up, hurry up. Let's get this over with as quick le as we can, because they will be on their way already." And he was referring to the volunteers, who would have posed a danger to this operation. I tried to calm him down. I said: "There's no need to be afraid. I didn't come here alone, you see. I brought the military police with me." But you just couldn't calm him down. He was agitated. And we entered the TO staff immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think this is probably a matter of translation, but three times - and we just heard it right now - in English, we're saying the TO staff. Now, "staff" has a connotation of people who work somewhere, but it seems that what the witness is talking about is the TO building. Can we just have a clarification? Because from page 60, on line 23, we have "TO staff," page 61, line 3, we have "TO staff," and just now - I can't find the line, but - yes, line 11 on page 61, when we have the same expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talked about the TO staff, you were referring to the building, the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was outside the TO building and the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can we please continue now.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my attempt to calm Simo down, when I told him that we would pull it off and that there wouldn't be any trouble, well, let me tell you, I myself was pretty scared. I have no idea what I would have done had those people stumbled upon us. We entered the TO building. They unlocked the door to the room where those people were being kept. Simo Zaric stood in the door. It was already getting dark and there was no lighting in the building or in the police station, or in the TO building. There was no electricity. There was a power cut, a power failure, all over the town. Simo stood in the doorway and spoke to the detainees in the room. He told them not to be afraid. He told them we were there, the army, and that we would take them to the Brcko garrison, where they would be safe. He told them that this was being done for their own safety. "Look at what they're doing to you here, how they're treating you, and once we take you there, you will be left well alone. No one will be mistreating you there." They simply -- well, they -- I was standing behind Simo. All I could see were silhouettes, and I didn't even know those people, hardly anyone. I may have seen some of them before, but ... There was commotion in the room. They asked no questions. When Simo explained this, all they said -- someone from the group spoke up and said: "Thank you, Simo." And Simo told Mile Topolovac to start gathering these people so that we could leave as soon as possible. Topolovac called out their names. I was on my way out back in the street. I was afraid that the members of special forces would come. I didn't want anything bad to happen. And then when I came back, Topolovac was using a lamp, a torch, to call out names from a list. We didn't verify the people's identity. We didn't check who was coming onto the truck. I didn't even count them. There was no way for us to ID those people, but Simo knew most of those people, and as they were passing, they knew who the people were. Some people had been brought over from the police station, and they too boarded the vehicles. Once they were in the vehicles and we were about to leave, Simo spoke to them again, telling them not to do anything stupid. He told them again that it was for their own safety, that we were now taking them to Brcko, and he warned all of them against trying to jump off any of the vehicles, because we were being escorted by military police. He warned these people against putting themselves in danger, themselves or anyone else, because part of the military police -- part of the task of the military police was to prevent people from escaping. So people were warned about this. Another brief warning was given to them and then we headed off to Brcko. None of the volunteers appeared, and that was good. We left the town of Samac safely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Could I -- Mr. Pisarevic, could I ask a short question in connection with these events? You just walked into the TO building and the police station, meeting no resistance from the policemen or the guards on duty? They just let you in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nobody questioned that. Most probably the person on duty was probably one of these police officers, whether it was Savo Cancarevic or Topolovac, and Simo had probably made an agreement with them that we would come, so they knew about it. Stevan Todorovic was not in Samac at that time. Maybe Simo had such information and he wanted to do it on that day. Perhaps he had the information that there wasn't a larger group of these Sareni in Samac on that day, and that is why we picked that day for the transfer. I don't know. I don't have information about where Stevan was or anything like that. But nobody from the police prevented us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Simo Zaric go together with you as you were escorting these people to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Simo didn't come with me. Simo stayed in Samac. Savo Cancarevic and Topolovac also stayed behind. Only I went along with the military police, the same people that I came with. We went to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Brcko, to the barracks, could you please describe to us what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to say that already in the village of Loncari when I left the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group and we were entering into the zone of responsibility of the 395th Motorised Brigade, I took a part of the police officers and told them to take a vehicle and go to the Pelagicevo command post. Another part of the military police went to Brcko, because I assessed that there was no longer any danger from the people that I was afraid of originally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us now what happened at the Brcko barracks when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to the Brcko barracks, we were told where to go at the entrance by a military police officer. They were expecting us, and they knew that we were coming. They told us to go to the premises where these people that we were bringing would be accommodated. Since I had worked in the Brcko barracks, I could see that they were not sending them to the prison or to the detention section which existed in the barracks. It was small; that is true. They sent us to a building where the company warehouses were. This is where the military police officer told us to go. When we came in front of those buildings, the lights were switched off in front of the building, so the front of the buildings were not lit, but there was light inside the buildings, and I was surprised to see masks on the faces of the military policemen. This surprised me, because I didn't know the reason for this, but I didn't ask any questions either why they were wearing those masks. They were wearing those caps which you pull over your face and which have openings only for the mouth and for the eyes so that you could breathe. I guess they're used so that the persons wearing them would not be recognised. After that, the prisoners that we had brought were ordered to come out of the vehicles, to line up, and to enter the rooms that were allocated for them. Then, again, I had another surprise. As they were entering, the military police was also inside. There was light now in those rooms. And those prisoners were received in a rough manner. They were searched using the police methods where they would place their hands on the wall, spread their legs, and then they were searched. Before that, there were also some blows administered. And particularly when I noticed that the people who were searched then had their hands tied behind their back. So they were tied and then they were brought into the room. I was very surprised, because I know what our agreement was. We were going to save these people, to spare them further abuse. And as soon as they came in, the same thing began.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have run out of time now, so I would like to ask you to stop and we will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall rise and continue our proceedings on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 28th day of February 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
